ecology.title: The Guardian of the Dry Forest
ecology.subtitle: An ancestral symbiosis etched in scarlet feathers.
ecology.content: The Scarlet Macaw is not just an inhabitant; it is the architect of the canopy. In the rigor of the Guanacaste dry forest, its existence is tied to giants like the Ceiba and the Tempisque. As a seed disperser and occupant of natural cavities, its presence dictates the health and future of local biodiversity.
ecology.quote: Its flight is not just a spectacle of color, it is the vital pulse of an ecosystem that refuses to disappear.

cards.title: Cavity Dependency
cards.description: They depend on mature trees with pre-existing cavities for nesting, making them vulnerable to logging.

cards.title: Species in Symbiosis
cards.description: They actively interact with hundreds of botanical species, acting as gardeners of the dry forest.

cards.title: Biological Corridor
cards.description: Their current distribution range spans the Guanacaste biological corridor, a fragmented but restoring habitat.

threats.title: Silent Threats
threats.subtitle: An ecosystem in precarious balance.
threats.content: The fragmentation of the dry forest and illegal nest poaching have pushed the Scarlet Macaw to the brink of the abyss. It is not just about the loss of space; it is the interruption of life cycles spanning decades.
threats.quote: Every fallen tree is one less nest, a generation lost in the forest echo.

01.title: Illegal Poaching
01.description: The trafficking of chicks for the pet market remains an open wound in conservation.

02.title: Habitat Loss
02.description: Agricultural and livestock expansion drastically reduces safe nesting sites.

03.title: Climate Change
03.description: Prolonged droughts affect fruit availability and chick survival.

recovery.title: The Path of Return
recovery.subtitle: Science and community in action for life.
recovery.content: The recovery of the Scarlet Macaw in Guanacaste is one of the greatest conservation successes in the dry tropics. Through artificial nests and constant monitoring, we have managed to reverse a trend that seemed irreversible.
recovery.quote: Conservation is not just saving a species, it is restoring the symphony of the forest.

sightseeing.title: Ethical Sighting
sightseeing.subtitle: Observing without intervening is the greatest act of respect.
sightseeing.content: The Scarlet Macaw is a sensitive species. Your presence must be invisible for their behavior to remain natural. Follow these guidelines to ensure your encounter is positive for both you and the birds.
dos: Maintain a minimum distance of 20 meters.
Wear neutral colors that blend with the forest.
Speak quietly and avoid sudden movements.
donts: Do not feed the birds under any circumstances.
Do not use flashes or intense lights.
Do not play bird call recordings (playback).
Do not attempt to touch or chase individuals.

anatomy.title: Beak anatomy of the scarlet macaw (Ara macao)
anatomy.summary: The beak of the scarlet macaw is large, strong, and curved, adapted to break hard-shelled seeds and fruits. It is formed by a bone structure covered in keratin, a resistant material that protects the beak from wear.
steps: Holds the seed with the beak and, occasionally, with one of its feet.
Applies pressure using its powerful mandibular muscles.
Fractures the shell thanks to the curved and robust shape of the beak.
Extracts and consumes the nutritious content, discarding the remains.
anatomy.details: The scarlet macaw possesses highly developed mandibular muscles that generate a great bite force. This specialized adaptation represents an evolutionary advantage to exploit food resources that other birds cannot consume.

conservation.title: Habitat and conservation in the dry tropics
conservation.summary: The Ara macao inhabits the tropical dry forests of the Pacific of Costa Rica, where it depends on large trees for nesting and a wide variety of fruits and seeds for feeding. Although its populations have recovered in some areas thanks to conservation efforts, it still faces threats such as habitat loss, logging of nesting trees, and illegal wildlife trafficking. Forest protection, reforestation with native species, and nest monitoring are fundamental actions to guarantee its survival.
